subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Why is good customer service important to a business?
options: It can increase customer loyalty and repeat business
It guarantees lower wages
It always lowers costs to zero
It removes the need to sell products
questions.explain: Good customer service encourages loyalty and repeat purchases, helping sales and reputation.

questions.q: Procurement in operations refers to:
options: Paying wages to staff
Selling finished goods to customers
Sourcing and buying the materials and supplies a business needs
Advertising the product
questions.explain: Procurement is the process of finding suppliers and purchasing the inputs a business needs.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an internal economy of scale?
options: A fall in industry-wide transport costs
A government grant to all firms
Lower interest rates for everyone
Purchasing economies from buying materials in bulk at a lower unit price
questions.explain: Bulk buying lowers the unit cost of materials, which is an internal (purchasing) economy of scale.

questions.q: Job production is best described as:
options: Producing one-off, customised products to a specific order
Making identical products on a continuous line
Producing goods entirely by machine
Making products in groups or sets
questions.explain: Job production makes single, often customised items, such as a tailored suit or a bridge.

questions.q: A reliable supply chain is important because it:
options: Removes the need for stock control
Increases the chance of running out of stock
Ensures materials and products are available when needed
Always raises selling prices
questions.explain: An efficient supply chain ensures the right materials and goods are available at the right time.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of Just In Time (JIT) stock management?
options: Reduced money tied up in stock and lower storage costs
No reliance on suppliers
Large buffer stocks at all times
High storage and insurance costs
questions.explain: JIT lowers the cash tied up in stock and reduces storage costs, but it relies on reliable suppliers.

questions.q: Batch production involves:
options: Producing only by hand
Making a single unique product
Continuous production that never stops
Making groups of similar products together before switching to another batch
questions.explain: Batch production makes a quantity of one product, then switches to make a batch of another, e.g. bread.

questions.q: A business that achieves higher productivity is likely to benefit from:
options: Lower average costs per unit and improved competitiveness
Higher average costs per unit
More waste
Slower production
questions.explain: Greater productivity spreads costs over more output, lowering average cost per unit and improving competitiveness.

questions.q: What is productivity?
options: The total cost of production
The total amount of stock held
Output produced per unit of input (e.g. per worker) in a given time
The number of customers served
questions.explain: Productivity measures output per input, such as the number of units produced per worker per hour.

questions.q: A key feature of lean production is to:
options: Increase the number of defective products
Minimise waste of all kinds while maintaining quality
Use only manual labour
Hold as much stock as possible
questions.explain: Lean production focuses on cutting waste (time, materials, stock) while keeping quality high.

questions.q: A buffer stock is held mainly to:
options: Remove the need for any suppliers
Increase the chance of running out of materials
Provide a reserve of stock in case of delays or higher-than-expected demand
Reduce the quality of products
questions.explain: Buffer (minimum) stock is a safety reserve to avoid running out if demand rises or deliveries are delayed.

questions.q: Economies of scale lead to:
options: A fall in average cost per unit as output increases
No change in costs
A rise in average cost per unit as output increases
Higher costs for all firms
questions.explain: Economies of scale mean the average cost per unit falls as a business produces on a larger scale.

questions.q: Introducing technology such as robotics into operations may have the drawback of:
options: Making quality impossible to measure
Producing less consistent output
Lower productivity
High initial purchase and installation costs, and possible job losses
questions.explain: Automation can raise productivity but involves high set-up costs and may reduce the need for some workers.

questions.q: Which statement about the supply chain is correct?
options: It only includes the final customer
It is the same as the marketing mix
It covers all the stages and businesses involved in getting a product from raw materials to the consumer
It refers only to advertising
questions.explain: The supply chain links every stage and business involved in moving a product from raw materials to the end consumer.

questions.q: Efficiency in operations means:
options: Producing output using the fewest resources and least waste
Holding maximum stock
Always producing the cheapest possible product
Hiring as many workers as possible
questions.explain: Efficiency means getting the most output from the available inputs while minimising waste.

questions.q: Which is a benefit of using technology such as automation in operations?
options: It can increase productivity and consistency
It removes the need for any quality control
It increases waste
It always reduces output
questions.explain: Automation can raise productivity and produce more consistent output, though it has set-up costs.

questions.q: What does Just In Time (JIT) stock management aim to do?
options: Increase storage costs
Never reorder materials
Keep stock levels to a minimum, with materials arriving as needed
Hold very large stocks at all times
questions.explain: JIT keeps stock to a minimum, with supplies arriving just as they are needed, reducing storage costs.

questions.q: What is a likely drawback of flow (mass) production?
options: It cannot produce large quantities
It always produces poor quality
High set-up costs and limited ability to customise products
It is only suitable for one-off items
questions.explain: Flow production has high initial set-up costs and produces standardised goods, limiting customisation.

questions.q: What is a drawback of holding too much stock (overstocking)?
options: Money tied up in stock and higher storage and waste costs
Always faster sales
Lower storage costs
Better cash flow
questions.explain: Holding excess stock ties up cash and increases storage, insurance and potential wastage costs.

questions.q: On a bar gate stock control chart, the reorder level is the point at which:
options: Production must stop permanently
Stock falls to zero
Stock reaches its maximum
A new order for stock should be placed
questions.explain: The reorder level is the stock level that triggers a new order, allowing for the supplier's lead time.

questions.q: What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?
options: Quality assurance ignores customers
They are identical
Quality control checks products at the end; quality assurance builds quality into the whole process
Quality control happens only after sale
questions.explain: Quality control inspects finished goods, while quality assurance builds quality in at every stage.

questions.q: Flow production is most suitable for:
options: Hand-made furniture
Custom wedding cakes
Mass-producing large quantities of identical, standardised products
Unique one-off items
questions.explain: Flow (mass) production continuously makes large quantities of identical products, e.g. cars or canned drinks.
